subject.title: O-Jazz-O War Memoir: Jazz, Don’t Listen To It At Your Own Risk
subject.author: Bob Kaufman
subject.text:
In the beginning, in the wet
Warm dark place,
Straining to break out, clawing at strange cables
Hearing her screams, laughing
" Later we forgave ourselves, we didn't know"
Some secret jazz
Shouted, wait, don't go.
Impatient, we came running, innocent
Laughing blobs of blood & faith.
To this mother, father world
Where laughter seems out of place
So we learned to cry, pleased
They pronounce human.
The secret Jazz blew a sigh
Some familiar sound shouted wait
Some are evil, some will hate.
"Just Jazz, blowing its top again"
So we rushed & laughed.
As we pushed & grabbed
While jazz blew in the night
Suddenly they were too busy to hear a simple sound
They were busy shoving mud in men's mouths,
Who were busy dying on the living ground
Busy earning medals, for killing children on deserted street corners
Occupying their fathers, raping their mothers, busy humans we
Busy burning Japanese in atomicolorcinemascope
With stereophonic screams,
What one hundred per cent red blooded savage, would waste precious
            time
Listening to jazz, with so many important things going on
But even the fittest murderers must rest
So they sat down in our blood soaked garments,
and listened to jazz
            lost, steeped in all our death dreams
They were shocked at the sound of life, long gone from our own
They were indignant at the whistling, thinking, singing, beating,
            swinging,
They wept for it, hugged, kissed it, loved it, joined it, we drank it,
Smoked it, ate with it, slept with it
They made our girls wear it for lovemaking
Instead of silly lace gowns,
Now in those terrible moments, when the dark memories come
The secret moments to which we admit no one
When guiltily we crawl back in time, reaching away from ourselves
They hear a familiar sound,
Jazz, scratching, digging, blueing, swinging jazz,
And listen,
And feel, & die.

title: Nothing About This Poet Holds Still, Least of All the Poem
standfirst: Bob Kaufman took a ten-year vow of silence, is credited by one source with a word he may never have coined, and spent sixteen years quietly rewriting a single poem about jazz and mass killing. His biographers cannot even agree on how old he was when he first went to sea.

sections.heading: A Vow Kept for a Decade, Then Broken Twice
sections.body: When television showed John F. Kennedy dying in Dallas in November 1963, Bob Kaufman stopped talking. He treated it as a Buddhist vow rather than a breakdown: a total withdrawal from speech and from writing, sustained for years while he lived, largely unrecorded, around San Francisco's North Beach. [Wikipedia dates the vow's end to 1973](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Bob_Kaufman), with Kaufman walking into a coffee shop to recite a new poem, "All Those Ships that Never Sailed." [The Academy of American Poets gives 1975 instead](https://poets.org/poet/bob-kaufman), a date Encyclopaedia Britannica repeats independently, tying the moment to the actual end of the Vietnam War rather than the 1973 Paris cease-fire that stopped direct American combat. Neither account explains the two-year gap; the sources simply disagree. What they do agree on is what came after: in 1978, having spoken again for a few years, Kaufman [went silent a second time](https://www.britannica.com/biography/Bob-Kaufman), a silence he broke only rarely for the rest of his life. A poet willing to shut down his own voice twice, on purpose, for years at a stretch, is not a promising subject for a tidy biography. As it turns out, he doesn't get one.

sections.heading: The Word Beatnik, and Who Gets Credit
sections.body: [One Academy of American Poets essay states plainly that Kaufman "is credited with coining the term 'beatnik'"](https://poets.org/text/bob-kaufman-enigmatic-beat-poet), the label that turned the Beat Generation into a marketable joke. The standard history says otherwise. San Francisco Chronicle columnist Herb Caen put the word into print for the first time on 2 April 1958, welding "Beat" to the "-nik" suffix that Sputnik had just made fashionable, to describe [a Look magazine party for "50 Beatniks" in a North Beach house](https://allenginsberg.org/2010/03/and-wherever-did-that-pesky-term-beatnik-come-from/). [Wikipedia's own dedicated entry on the word credits Caen alone](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Beatnik) and never mentions Kaufman. The Academy of American Poets' own shorter biographical page doesn't repeat the coining claim either — it simply isn't there. Two pages published by the same organization disagree about a fact any newspaper archive could settle, and the disagreement sits there uncorrected.

sections.heading: A Childhood That Depends on Which Page You Read
sections.body: [Wikipedia states it plainly: "Born in New Orleans, Kaufman was the 10th of 13 children. His paternal grandfather was a German Jew, and his mother was from an established Black, Roman Catholic New Orleans family."](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Bob_Kaufman) [Encyclopaedia Britannica describes the same childhood differently](https://www.britannica.com/biography/Bob-Kaufman): "a Roman Catholic mother, a German-Jewish father, and a grandmother who believed in voodoo" — the Jewish ancestor has moved up a generation, from grandfather to father. [A research profile from EBSCO moves the mother again](https://www.ebsco.com/research-starters/history/bob-kaufman/), describing her as a Black Catholic woman from Martinique rather than New Orleans, and counts Kaufman as the eleventh of thirteen children rather than the tenth. [The magazine Beatdom, attempting its own account, gives up trying to adjudicate](https://www.beatdom.com/bob-kaufman-the-unsung-beat/) and admits its version is "drawn from an extremely wide selection of reading, containing a number of conflicting dates and stories." Even the age at which Kaufman went to sea won't hold still: Wikipedia says eighteen; Britannica says thirteen, and adds that he survived four shipwrecks and permanent hearing loss along the way. None of this is a matter of interpretation. These are counting errors, and nobody agrees on how to correct them.

sections.heading: Twenty Years at Sea, a Different Kind of Politics
sections.body: Whatever age he actually left home, Kaufman spent years in the Merchant Marine before he wrote a line anyone kept. [He joined the National Maritime Union, opposed the anti-communist purges that gutted it during the McCarthy years, and drew FBI surveillance that reportedly continued until 1970](https://www.musicandliterature.org/reviews/2020/7/5/bob-kaufmans-collected-poems) — a decade after he had supposedly already stopped speaking to anyone. He eventually left the sea for New York, enrolling at the New School for Social Research, where he met William S. Burroughs and Allen Ginsberg. Even this meeting resists a single account: one retrospective has Kaufman first reaching San Francisco with his brother Donald as early as 1950, [while another has him arriving later, with Burroughs and Ginsberg, once the three had already become friends in New York](https://brooklynrail.org/2019/09/books/Eternal-Poet). Wikipedia settles on 1958 as the year he moved into North Beach for good. Whichever version is true, North Beach is where he stayed, performing his poems aloud in bars and on the street rather than submitting them anywhere — the reason so much of what survives exists only because his second wife, Eileen, wrote it down as he spoke it.

sections.heading: A Poem He Kept Taking Back
sections.body: "O-Jazz-O" is not one poem so much as one poem Kaufman never stopped rewriting. [Its earliest mass publication was in Solitudes Crowded with Loneliness, the 1965 New Directions collection assembled from his wife Eileen's transcriptions](https://openspace.sfmoma.org/2017/11/bob-kaufmans-african-dream/), where it ran under the plainer title "War Memoir." [A version of the same poem appears in all three books published in his lifetime](https://www.musicandliterature.org/reviews/2020/7/5/bob-kaufmans-collected-poems) — Solitudes in 1965, [Golden Sardine, the twenty-first title in City Lights' Pocket Poets series, in 1967](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/City_Lights_Pocket_Poets_Series), and The Ancient Rain in 1981 — meaning Kaufman kept returning to these same lines about jazz and mass killing across sixteen years bracketing both his vow of silence and its end. Along the way its warning flipped its meaning entirely: [what began as "Jazz — listen to it at your own risk" became, in a later version, "Jazz — don't listen to it at your own risk"](https://openspace.sfmoma.org/2017/11/bob-kaufmans-african-dream/), the form printed above. That exact wording was only fixed in place in Cranial Guitar, the 1996 Coffee House Press collection assembled a decade after Kaufman's death — so the words a reader now sees are not simply what Kaufman first wrote, but the last of several versions he left behind, settled on after he could no longer be asked which one he meant. Inside the poem, the violence the jazz answers is named without euphemism: people "Busy burning Japanese in atomicolorcinemascope / With stereophonic screams," dying and killing on "the living ground" while a culture too occupied with murder to listen finally sits down, exhausted, and listens anyway.

sections.heading: What the Collections Never Quite Settle
sections.body: Kaufman [published only three full-length collections in his lifetime and, by preference, favoured recitation on the street and in bars](https://www.musicandliterature.org/reviews/2020/7/5/bob-kaufmans-collected-poems) over anything fixed on a page. Cranial Guitar, the 1996 book that gave "O-Jazz-O" its now-standard title, [won the PEN Center USA West award the following year](https://www.ebsco.com/research-starters/history/cranial-guitar-bob-kaufman). City Lights finally gathered everything into [The Collected Poems of Bob Kaufman in November 2019](https://www.musicandliterature.org/reviews/2020/7/5/bob-kaufmans-collected-poems), edited by Neeli Cherkovski, Raymond Foye, and Tate Swindell, with a foreword by the poet devorah major — who, writing about the same book elsewhere, [described its subject as "a man steeped in a mythology sprinkled with a few facts"](https://brooklynrail.org/2019/09/books/Eternal-Poet). That is as close to a settled verdict as Kaufman's record seems able to produce, even from someone who helped assemble it: a poet who named his son after Charlie Parker, who is credited by some with inventing the word used to mock his own movement, and who died of emphysema on 12 January 1986 in the city he had spent thirty years talking about, and twice refused to talk in at all.
